First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4x+3 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+({2}^{2}-{2}^{2})+3 \\  & =({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2})-4+3 \\  & =(x+2)^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
{\int }_{-2+2/\sqrt{3}}^{0}\frac{3}{|x+2|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4x+3}}\,\text{d}x=3{\int }_{-2+2/\sqrt{3}}^{0}\frac{1}{|x+2|\sqrt{(x+2)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}\,u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x+2).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x+2.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-2+\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ | $2$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2+2/\sqrt{3}}^{0}\frac{3}{|x+2|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4x+3}}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{2/\sqrt{3}}^{2}\frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\,\text{arcsec}\,u\,{|}_{2/\sqrt{3}}^{2} \\  & =3(\text{arcsec}(2)-\text{arcsec}\,(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}})) \\  & =3(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
